newsitem.title: USA: Bonneville, British Columbia settle hydro dispute.
newsitem.headline: Bonneville, British Columbia settle hydro dispute.

text.p: Bonneville Power Administration (BPA) and the province of British Columbia have settled a dispute over the Columbia River Treaty, with B.C. agreeing to accept power instead of cash as payment.
Under the agreement in principle reached in late November, BPA is also released from earlier commitments to construct new transmission lines, Bonneville said.

BPA, an agency of the U.S. government which markets hydroelectric power in the Pacific Northwest, last year pulled out of a 1994 deal to pay $180 million in exchange for reducing Canada's annual capacity entitlement by one-third to 950 megawatts (MW).

Bonneville had also agreed to buy the remainder of Canada's treaty entitlement at market rates between 1998 and 2024, but cited drastic restructuring of the power industry and lower-than-expected wholesale prices for its change of heart.
Under the Columbia River Treaty, signed in 1961, Canada is entitled to around 1,400 megawatts of capacity and 550 average megawatts of energy.
In the 1960's, Canada did not need the additional power and sold its share to a consortium of utilities under a 30-year contract, expiring in stages from 1998 to 2003.
The contract was timed to expire in line with the scheduled construction, paid for by the U.S., of three new dams in Canada and one in the U.S., which have since been indefinitely postponed.
The new agreement allows BPA to return the Canadian entitlement to B.C. using existing transmission lines, without the addition of extra transmission charges.
The power is still expected to be re-sold, mainly to U.S. utilities and marketers, since B.C. produces much more power than it uses, market sources noted.
The recent agreement does not address the issue of the excess capacity and energy in the U.S., but a commercial agreement is expected before July 1, 1997, according to Bonneville.
